newsitem.title: USA: NYSE stocks trade in increments of one-sixteenths.
newsitem.headline: NYSE stocks trade in increments of one-sixteenths.

text.p: Stocks on the New York Stock Exchange traded in increments of 1/16, or 6.25 cents, for the first time on Tuesday, breaking from the exchange's past practice of intervals of 1/8, or 12.5 cents.
An NYSE spokeswoman said the transition went smoothly, although some traders said it would take some time to get used to the narrower spreads between bid and asked prices.
"I have not had a problem today with any of my orders," said James Volk, director of equity trading at Jensen Securities.
"A couple of guys are saying it's the worst thing in the world, other guys are saying it hasn't hurt them at all," Volk said.
Nasdaq and the American Stock Exchange earlier adopted trading in sixteenths.
The move could favour small investors by allowing them to buy stocks at lower prices and sell at higher prices.

Traders said, however, that on thinly traded stocks, the narrower spreads between bid and ask prices could significantly pinch profits for market makers, the traders who fill public orders for stocks.
"On the most liquid stocks it's a real positive; on the thinner stocks it's kind of a wait-and-see," said Peter Coolidge, senior equity trader at Brean Murray & Co.
The move to sixteenths was seen as a step towards Wall Street eventually trading stocks in decimals instead of fractions, which is being weighed by exchanges.
"I think it's just a step before decimalization, to see how it works," said Kenneth Ducey, vice president, director of trading, BT Brokerage.
